caveats: The mediation result carries the contextual net-other-channel sign condition already present in the paper; it does not establish that sign empirically, and cancellation examples refute only an unconditional extension of the comparison.

The general mediation theorem uses an arbitrary probability measure with the five specified potential variables integrable; independent assignment and consistency are realized by a product Bernoulli law and the observed-variable definitions.

The IV repair is for finite populations with arbitrary probability weights, knowledge values in a bounded natural-number range, and arbitrary real response functions; its estimand averages dose increments at crossed margins rather than necessarily each increaser’s entire knowledge-change effect.
The IV counterexamples are finite constructions respecting the recorded knowledge and support ranges; they neither assert actual knowledge decreasers nor change the reported empirical estimates.

The displayed index correction for stratum indicators is also formalized as finite regression algebra, without an identification or estimation claim for the treatment coefficient; P043-T3 remains contextual prose rather than a separate mathematical theorem.

corrections.what: Randomized curriculum assignment and exclusion alone do not justify the printed identification of the effect among knowledge increasers: finite models have a positive first stage and zero IV ratio despite increaser effect one, or identical full observable laws with increaser effects one and $4/3$.

The printed local-effect claim has a corrected finite-population reading under individual knowledge monotonicity: with independent nondegenerate assignment, exclusion, consistency, bounded integer knowledge and a positive first stage, the IV ratio is a nonnegative, unit-sum weighted average of one-unit causal increments over crossed knowledge margins.

key_results.what: Under independent nondegenerate binary assignment, consistency and integrable mediation potentials, the total contrast is $\tau=M+D$ and $\tau\ge M$ holds exactly when the net other-channel effect $D\ge0$, with the corresponding linear-model identities also proved.

overview.overview: This curriculum experiment studies how knowledge of civil liberties relates to support for them, using randomized curriculum assignment and an instrumental-variable interpretation. The Lean development proves the mediation decomposition and its contextual sign comparison for arbitrary integrable populations, constructs finite counterexamples to local-effect identification without knowledge monotonicity, and proves a monotone integer-dose IV repair. These are population identities and identification statements, not a reanalysis of the estimated curriculum effects.

text.body: The sentence on p. 474 refers back to the positive-other-channel scenario on p. 473. The Lean statement gives two models showing why extending that conditional comparison to every randomized design would fail. These are my examples and are not in the paper. They violate the hypothesized sign premise; they do not refute the paper’s contextual conditional. Each model is a finite set of equally likely states, 8 in the first and 1000 in the second. For each model the statement asserts the population quantities described below. The curriculum raises knowledge by $6/5$ on average, and a one-point increase in knowledge from 8 or from 9 raises expected support by $1/20$ at either assignment. Writing $K(t)$ and $S(t,k)$ for potential knowledge and support, the effect through knowledge is $M = \mathbb{E}[S(0,K(1))-S(0,K(0))] = 3/50$, the net effect through the other channels is $D = \mathbb{E}[S(1,K(1))-S(0,K(1))] = -3/50$, and the reduced form is $\tau = 0$. The statement asserts also that the assignment is a fair coin independent of the student’s type, and that the observed support score has the same distribution in the two arms. In the second model, knowledge is 8, 9 or 10, support is 2 or 3, and a score for general political knowledge is 2 under both assignments. The statement concerns the population contrasts of these two models, each with a single stratum. It asserts nothing about the estimates of Table 4 or about the sign of $D$ in the experiment.
text.headline: Two counterexamples to an unconditional extension of the mediation comparison
text.location: Results, p. 474 (PDF p. 12), left column below Table 4; the passage that the sentence refers to is on p. 473 (PDF p. 11), left column

text.body: The population has an arbitrary probability law, and assignment is an independent Bernoulli draw with probability $p$, where $0<p<1$. Observed knowledge and support follow consistency, $K=K(T)$ and $S=S(T,K(T))$, in an acyclic model with well-defined interventions on knowledge. The five variables $K(0)$, $K(1)$, $A=S(1,K(1))$, $B=S(0,K(1))$ and $C=S(0,K(0))$ have finite expectations. I write $M = \mathbb{E}[S(0,K(1))-S(0,K(0))]$ for the contrast through knowledge and $D = \mathbb{E}[S(1,K(1))-S(0,K(1))]$ for the net contrast through the other channels. With $\tau=\mathbb{E}[S\mid T=1]-\mathbb{E}[S\mid T=0]$, the comparison is $\tau=\mathbb{E}[A]-\mathbb{E}[C]=M+D$, $\tau\ge M\iff D\ge0$ and $\tau>M\iff D>0$. The pointwise decomposition uses the same $B$ in both differences. If $D\ge0$ and $\tau\le0$, then $M\le0$, including when $\tau=0$. In the additive linear model with integrable disturbances, the first stage is $a$, $M=ab$, $D=c$ and $\tau=ab+c$; for $a>0$, $\tau/a=b+c/a$ and $\tau/a\ge b\iff c\ge0$. For finitely many additive other channels, the comparison depends on their net sum: nonnegativity of every channel is sufficient but not necessary. These are population comparisons; they leave the sign of the other-channel contribution in the experiment unspecified.
text.headline: The mediation comparison with its contextual sign condition made explicit
text.location: Results, p. 474 (PDF p. 12), left column below Table 4; Statistical Model, p. 473 (PDF p. 11), left column

text.body: The passage is interpretive prose rather than a formal inequality. It defines neither “biased in favor” nor “mediating relationship”, but its words “as noted above” refer to the hypothesized positive effects through other channels on p. 473. Its natural reading therefore carries a sign premise and does not assert that randomization alone guarantees the comparison. Writing the reduced-form contrast as $\tau = M + D$, with $M$ the effect through knowledge and $D$ the net effect through other channels, gives $\tau \ge M$ when $D \ge 0$. My two cancellation examples have $D < 0$ and refute only an unconditional extension of this comparison; they do not refute the paper’s contextual conditional or determine the sign in the experiment. The clause on the power of the experiment is outside this comparison and was not formalized.
text.headline: The sentence beginning “This pattern of results is striking”, as printed
text.location: Results, p. 474 (PDF p. 12), left column below Table 4; the passage that the sentence refers to is on p. 473 (PDF p. 11), left column

text.body: The Lean statement covers the two parts of the counterexample in P043-E002, whose populations are mine and are not in the paper. In each population the assignment $Z$ is a fair coin independent of the student’s type, and the support $Y(k)$ depends only on the type and on the integer knowledge score. For the population of the table in that finding, the statement asserts that the first stage is $1/3$, that the mean of support is $10/3$ in both arms, and that the instrumental-variable ratio is $0$. It asserts also that the students whose knowledge rises are exactly those of the first type, and that each has the effect $Y(9) - Y(8) = 1$. The second part gives two populations, each with five types of equal probability. A type is written $(K(0), K(1), Y)$ with $H(k) = \mathbf{1}\{k \ge 9\}$, and the responses 2 and 4 are constant: $\begin{aligned} A&:\ (8,9,3+H),\ (8,9,3+H),\ (9,8,2+2H),\ (8,8,2),\ (9,9,4),\\ B&:\ (8,9,3+H),\ (8,9,3+H),\ (9,8,2+2H),\ (8,9,2+2H),\ (9,8,2+2H). \end{aligned}$ The statement asserts that $A$ and $B$ have the same joint distribution of $(Z,K,Y)$, with first stage $1/5$ and reduced form $0$. It asserts that the average effect among the students whose knowledge rises is $1$ in $A$ and $4/3$ in $B$, and that no function of the joint distribution equals this average effect in both. In all three populations the scores lie in the 2008 ranges of Table 3, and support is nondecreasing in knowledge. The statement does not assert that the curriculum lowered any student’s knowledge.
text.headline: A counterexample to the statements on the local average treatment effect of knowledge
text.location: Statistical Model, p. 472 (PDF p. 10), foot of the left column to the top of the right column; Conclusion, pp. 474–475 (PDF pp. 12–13)

text.body: The Lean statement asserts the corrected statement of P043-E002, in the notation of that finding, for a finite set of students with arbitrary probability weights. The assignment has probability $p$ with $0 < p < 1$, and the scores $K_i(0)$ and $K_i(1)$ are integers between $0$ and an arbitrary bound $J$. By construction, the assignment is independent of the student, and the support $Y_i(k)$ depends only on the student and on the knowledge score. The hypotheses are that $K_i(1) \ge K_i(0)$ for every student and that $\mathbb{E}[K_i(1) - K_i(0)] > 0$. The statement asserts that the first stage and the reduced form are $\mathbb{E}[K_i(1) - K_i(0)]$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y_i(K_i(1)) - Y_i(K_i(0))]$, and that the ratio of $\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y)$ to $\operatorname{Cov}(Z,K)$ equals the instrumental-variable ratio. It asserts the two telescoping identities of the finding for every student, that the weights $w_j$ are nonnegative and sum to one, and that the instrumental-variable ratio is $\sum_{j} w_j\, \mathbb{E}\bigl[Y_i(j) - Y_i(j-1) \mid K_i(0) < j \le K_i(1)\bigr],$ where the sum is over the levels $j$ that are crossed with positive probability. A student whose knowledge does not rise enters at no level, and no condition is placed on the sign of the increments $Y_i(j) - Y_i(j-1)$. A further part does not assume monotonicity: for all scores between $0$ and $J$, the identities hold with $\mathbf{1}\{K_i(1) \ge j\} - \mathbf{1}\{K_i(0) \ge j\}$ in place of the indicator of $K_i(0) < j \le K_i(1)$. This difference equals $-1$ at a level that the student crosses downward. The Lean statement is narrower than the corrected statement in one respect: the population is finite.
text.headline: The statements on the local average treatment effect of knowledge, as corrected
text.location: Statistical Model, p. 472 (PDF p. 10), foot of the left column to the top of the right column; Conclusion, pp. 474–475 (PDF pp. 12–13)

text.body: The Lean statement records what the corrected indices of equation (1) mean. The paper states the model and proves nothing about it, so the statement consists of the definition of $D_{ik}$ and of identities that follow from it. The identities are my unfolding of the corrected notation. Let there be $n$ students and $K \ge 1$ strata, let $s(i)$ be the stratum of student $i$, and let $D_{ik} = \mathbf{1}\{s(i) = k\}$ for $k = 1, \dots, K-1$, so that stratum $K$ is the reference stratum. For all real $\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_{K-1}$, the statement asserts that $\sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \gamma_k D_{ik}$ equals $\gamma_{s(i)}$ if $s(i) \le K-1$ and $0$ if $s(i) = K$, and that $\sum_{k=1}^{K-1} D_{ik} = 1 - \mathbf{1}\{s(i) = K\} .$ It asserts also that, for $X_i \in \{0,1\}$ and arbitrary real $Y_i$, $u_i$, $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$, the corrected equation (1) holds for every $i$ if and only if $Y_i = (\beta_0 + \gamma_{s(i)}) + \beta_1 X_i + u_i$ for every $i$, with the convention $\gamma_K = 0$. In words, the corrected model has an intercept for each stratum and one coefficient on the treatment. The assignment of students to strata is arbitrary, and the cases of a single stratum and of an empty set of students are included. The statement has the same scope as the corrected notation, and it asserts nothing about the interpretation of $\beta_1$ as an average treatment effect or about estimation.
